knitr::opts_chunk$set(

This page explains what each `repdist` function computes, in the order of a
typical analysis. Full argument lists are in the package help
(`?sample_mmd`, `?protein_similarity`, ...).

`embed_proteins()` returns an `AAStringSet` containing the protein sequences
and one learned representation per protein. In the examples below this object
is called `proteins` (in the help pages it is the argument `x`); the
embedding matrix is `S4Vectors::mcols(proteins)$embedding`, and $z_i$ is its
row for protein $i$.

| Name | Holds |
|---|---|
| `proteins` | sequences and their representations (`AAStringSet`) |
| `counts` | samples × proteins counts |
| `D` | distance between samples (`dist`) |
| `S` | protein × protein similarity graph (matrix) |
| `bins` | MCL result of `bin_proteins()` |
| `bin_counts` | samples × bins counts |

| Step | Function | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Representations | `embed_proteins()`, `read_embeddings()` | sequences, or a TM-Vec database | `proteins` |
| Sample distance | `sample_mmd()` | `counts`, `proteins` | `D` |
| Similarity graph | `protein_similarity()` | `proteins` | `S` |
| Protein bins | `bin_proteins()` | `S` | `bins` |
| Aggregation | `bin_glom()` | `counts`, `bins` | `bin_counts` |
| QC | `plot_tsne()`, `plot_bin_similarity()` | `proteins`, `bins`, `S` | ggplot objects |

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
library(ggplot2)
```

The executable examples use `simulate_cog`, the dataset shipped with the
package and used in [Get started](repdist.html): 110 proteins of the NCBI COG
2024 release with TM-Vec embeddings, ten of them GrpE (COG0576) from ten
different 30%-identity sequence clusters. [Simulated data](data_simulation.html)
shows how it was built.

```{r example-data}
data(simulate_cog, package = "repdist")
proteins <- simulate_cog$proteins
annotation <- simulate_cog$annotation
role <- setNames(annotation$role, annotation$protein)
table(role)
```

# Protein representations {#protein-representations}

Every other function takes the same object: an `AAStringSet` of protein
sequences, named by accession, with one embedding row per protein in
`mcols(proteins)$embedding`. Rows are unit-normalised.

```{r proteins}
proteins
dim(S4Vectors::mcols(proteins)$embedding)
```

There are two ways to get it.

**`embed_proteins()`: sequences to embeddings inside R.** It accepts a named
character vector, an `AAStringSet` or a FASTA path (read and checked by
`read_fasta()`), and a `model` key from `known_models()`. Models run in a
Python environment that `repdist` builds and pins itself through `basilisk`,
on a standalone Python it downloads, so users do not install Python, conda or
git. Weights are downloaded on first use and pinned to fixed revisions
(HuggingFace commits, or a SHA-256-checked file). Every sequence is embedded
whole; nothing is truncated or dropped.

```{r embed, eval = FALSE}
proteins <- embed_proteins("proteins.fasta") # model = "tmvec"
proteins <- embed_proteins(seqs, model = "esm2-650m", device = "cpu")
```

**`read_embeddings()`: embeddings computed elsewhere.** TM-Vec users can embed
outside R with the `tmvec` command-line tool
(<https://github.com/valentynbez/tmvec>) and import its `build-db` database
(`.npz`), giving the FASTA it was built from. An HDF5 file with one group per
protein (datasets `seq` and `emb`) is also read; per-residue embeddings are
averaged.

```{r read, eval = FALSE}
proteins <- read_embeddings("db/proteins.npz", seqs = "proteins.fasta")
```

**`known_models()`** lists the registered models. The default, `tmvec`, is a
TM-Vec head [@hamamsy2024tmvec] on the ProtT5-XL encoder
[@elnaggar2022prottrans]. Its head is trained so that the cosine similarity of
two embeddings predicts the TM-score of the two structures
[@zhang2004tmscore]; on this site, "predicted TM-score" means that cosine.
The `esm2-*` models give general sequence representations without this
calibration.

```{r models}
m <- known_models()
data.frame(
    model = names(m),
    backbone = vapply(m, `[[`, "", "backbone"),
    trained_to = vapply(m, function(s) s$training_max_length, 0),
    row.names = NULL
)
```

`trained_to` is the longest sequence in the model's training data. It is
recorded for reference and not enforced.

# Sample-level distance: MMD {#sample-level-distance-mmd}

`sample_mmd(counts, proteins)` treats sample $P$ as a weighted set of protein
embeddings $\{(z_i, p_i)\}$, where $p_i = c_i / \sum_j c_j$ is protein $i$'s
share of the sample's counts. Two samples are compared by the maximum mean
discrepancy [@gretton2012mmd; @muandet2017kme]:

$$
\mathrm{MMD}^2(P,Q) =
\sum_{i,j} p_i p_j\, k(z_i, z_j)
- 2 \sum_{i,j} p_i q_j\, k(z_i, z_j)
+ \sum_{i,j} q_i q_j\, k(z_i, z_j),
$$

with the Gaussian kernel on Euclidean distance

$$
k(z_i, z_j) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert z_i - z_j \rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
$$

The sums run over all proteins observed in either sample, and the function
returns $\mathrm{MMD}(P,Q)$ (the square root) as a `dist`. For unit-norm
embeddings $\lVert z_i - z_j \rVert^2 = 2(1 - s_{ij})$, where $s_{ij}$ is the
cosine similarity, so $k(z_i, z_j) = \exp(-(1 - s_{ij})/\sigma^2)$; with
TM-Vec, $s_{ij}$ is the predicted TM-score.

**Estimator.** This is the exact MMD between the observed
relative-abundance distributions, including within-sample diagonal terms.
When used to estimate population MMD, it is the biased plug-in form
[@gretton2012mmd, equation 5]. The unbiased U-statistic estimates squared
population MMD and can be negative; taking its square root would not give
a valid sample distance in those cases. Clipping negative values would
also lose unbiasedness. `sample_mmd()` therefore retains the empirical
distribution distance for PCoA and PERMANOVA. For integer counts, an
observation-level unbiased correction would also need to account for
repeated observations of the same protein; simply dropping the protein
kernel's diagonal is not that correction.

**Sampling depth.** Relative abundances remove total-count scaling, but
not depth-dependent sampling noise or changes in which proteins are seen.
Rarefaction is an optional analysis choice, not a requirement of the
distance. The vignette uses all observed counts as relative abundances;
the case study rarefies to a common depth before both distances. Raw
counts are retained for count-based differential abundance analysis.

**Why a kernel distance.** If $k$ were 1 for identical proteins and 0
otherwise, the returned MMD would reduce to the Euclidean distance between the
two relative-abundance vectors, an identity-only comparison. With the Gaussian
kernel, the cross term lets different accessions with close embeddings
partly match, in proportion to their abundances. MMD compares the two
weighted distributions through their kernel mean embeddings; unlike
optimal-transport distances it solves no transport problem and is computed
directly from the protein kernel matrix. The choice is methodological; it is
not a claim that transport-based distances cannot be used.

In the example, samples `s1` and `s2` share no accession but each holds five
GrpE proteins, while `s3` holds five background proteins:

```{r mmd-toy}
grpe <- names(role)[role == "GrpE"]
background <- names(role)[role == "background"]
counts <- matrix(0, 3, length(proteins),
    dimnames = list(c("s1", "s2", "s3"), names(proteins)))
counts["s1", grpe[1:5]] <- 10
counts["s2", grpe[6:10]] <- 10
counts["s3", background[1:5]] <- 10

D <- sample_mmd(counts, proteins)
D
vegan::vegdist(counts, "bray") # 1 for every pair: no shared accession
```

**Bandwidth.** With `sigma = NULL` (default), $\sigma$ is the median pairwise
Euclidean distance among the proteins observed in any sample (the median
heuristic). It therefore changes when samples bring in new proteins. The value
used is returned as `attr(D, "sigma")`; pass it back to hold the kernel fixed
across analyses. For TM-Vec embeddings, `sigma = sqrt(1 - t)` places the
kernel's $1/e$ point at predicted TM-score $t$.

```{r sigma}
attr(D, "sigma")
D2 <- sample_mmd(counts[1:2, ], proteins, sigma = attr(D, "sigma"))
```

`weighted = FALSE` gives every detected protein equal weight (a
presence/absence version). Before computing the kernel, `sample_mmd()` drops
proteins with zero abundance in every supplied sample. It then holds a dense
kernel over the union of proteins detected across the entire call, not a
separate kernel for each sample pair. Memory therefore grows with the square
of the retained protein count. One double-precision kernel alone takes
approximately $8r^2$ bytes for $r$ retained proteins; distance matrices and
temporary copies add to peak memory.

# Protein similarity graph {#protein-similarity-graph}

```
protein embeddings
        │  cosine similarity
pairwise similarity s_ij
        │  alignment E-value gate (E ≤ max_evalue)
weighted graph W
        │  Markov clustering
protein bins ── bin_glom() ──► samples × bins counts
```

## `protein_similarity()` {#protein-similarity}

`protein_similarity(proteins, max_evalue = 0.01)` returns the weighted
adjacency matrix

$$
W_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
s_{ij}, & s_{ij} > 0 \text{ and } E_{ij} \le E_{\max},\\
0, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
$$

where $s_{ij}$ is the cosine similarity of the embeddings (with TM-Vec, the
predicted TM-score), $E_{ij}$ the E-value of the two sequences' alignment and
$E_{\max}$ = `max_evalue`. There is no similarity threshold: the embeddings
only weight the edges, and the alignment decides which pairs are edges.

Every pair with a positive similarity is aligned locally (Smith-Waterman
[@smith1981local]; BLOSUM62, gap opening 11, extension 1). $E_{ij}$ is
BLAST's E-value for the shorter protein searched against all of `proteins`,
from the Karlin-Altschul statistics of BLOSUM62 with these gaps
($\lambda$ = 0.267, $K$ = 0.041) [@karlin1990evalue], without length
correction or composition-based statistics. The search space is the total
length of `proteins`, so one `max_evalue` is stricter on a larger set.
`max_evalue = Inf` skips the alignments and keeps every positive pair.

The number of alignments grows with the square of the number of proteins:
5,000 proteins take about 40 minutes on 10 cores (`n_cores`). The result is
an ordinary symmetric matrix (1 on the diagonal, 0 for every non-edge), so it
can be clustered by other graph algorithms as well; `bin_proteins()` is one
choice, not a requirement.

```{r similarity}
S <- protein_similarity(proteins)
c(proteins = nrow(S), edges = sum(S[upper.tri(S)] > 0))
```

# MCL clustering and aggregation {#mcl-clustering-and-aggregation}

## `bin_proteins()` {#bin-proteins}

`bin_proteins(S, inflation = 2)` partitions the graph by Markov clustering
(MCL) [@vandongen2000mcl]. MCL simulates random walks on the weighted graph,
alternating expansion (matrix powers) with inflation (elementwise powers
followed by renormalisation), so that flow concentrates within densely
connected regions. Clustering proteins by MCL on a pairwise-similarity network
goes back to TRIBE-MCL [@enright2002tribemcl] and OrthoMCL
[@li2003orthomcl]. Here, each connected component is clustered separately,
each protein's self-loop takes the weight of its heaviest edge (as in the
`mcl` program), and proteins without edges become singleton bins. Higher
inflation gives more, smaller bins.

```{r bins}
bins <- bin_proteins(S)
bins$graph
head(lengths(bins$clusters))
```

The result lists the members of each bin (`clusters`), each protein's bin
(`membership`), a medoid per bin (`representatives`), the `inflation` and a
summary of the graph (`graph`).

**The gate defines edges, not bins.** If A–B and B–C pass the E-value gate,
MCL can put A, B and C in one bin even when A–C does not. A bin therefore
does not guarantee that every pair of its members aligns significantly;
`plot_bin_similarity()` below shows which pairs inside a bin are edges.

## `bin_glom()` {#bin-glom}

`bin_glom(counts, bins)` sums the counts of each bin's members:

```
counts (samples × proteins) ──► membership ──► counts (samples × bins)
```

Sample totals are unchanged and a sparse `Matrix` stays sparse. Give it raw
counts when the next step is a count model such as DESeq2.

```{r glom}
bin_counts <- bin_glom(simulate_cog$counts, bins)
bin_counts[1:3, 1:5]
```

# QC and visualization {#qc-and-visualization}

## `plot_tsne()` {#plot-tsne}

`plot_tsne(proteins, color = NULL)` draws a two-dimensional t-SNE
[@vandermaaten2008tsne] of the embeddings computed on cosine distance,
$1 - s_{ij}$ (for TM-Vec, one minus the predicted TM-score). `color` takes
labels named by protein; the 12 most frequent are coloured. t-SNE preserves
local neighbourhoods, not distances between clusters or their sizes, and the
layout depends on the random seed.

```{r tsne, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1)
plot_tsne(proteins, color = role)
```

## `plot_bin_similarity()` {#plot-bin-similarity}

`plot_bin_similarity(bins, bin, S, proteins)` shows every pairwise similarity
among one bin's members. Cell colour is the similarity from the embeddings,
before any gate; a cross marks each pair that is not an edge of `S`. Crossed
pairs are in the bin through shared neighbours: their alignment failed the
E-value gate. Here, the bin holding the GrpE proteins:

```{r bin-similarity, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5}
grpe_bin <- names(which.max(table(bins$membership[grpe])))
plot_bin_similarity(bins, grpe_bin, S, proteins)
```
